newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says unfair polls will not aid Croatia loan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says unfair polls will not aid Croatia loan.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Monday called Croatia's weekend elections unfair and officials said this assessment will not help Zagreb's case for a $30 million World Bank loan that is expected to be decided later this month.

Albright, at a briefing news conference with her Bulgarian counterpart, said she agreed with monitors from the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) that the elections "may have been free but they were not fair."
She said opposition parties did not have full access to the media and they were other problems, including an assault an opposition candidates.

"We are concerned about the fact that there was not enough possibility for the opposition party to practice its ability to be part of the election," in which President Franjo Tudjman was elected to a new term of office, Albright said.

She reasserted that because of this and also because of U.S. dissastifaction with Zagreb's delay in complying with key aspects of the 1995 Dayton peace accords, the United States was vigilantly monitoring Croatia's every move.

Albright, on a trip to the Balkans two weeks ago, warned Croatia -- and also Serbia and Bosnian Serbs -- that they would not receive U.S. or international assistance if they refuse to comply with Dayton and other demands.
After that trip, Croatia took some "modest" steps to warrant the United States backing a $13 million loan to a Swiss company to renovate a cement plant in Croatia.
But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday Washington may block a $30 million World Bank loan to Croatia that is expected to be decided later this month.
"Each of these loans ... is going to be judged on a case-by-case basis" and there has been no decision yet on the $30 million loan, Burns told a news briefing.

But "it doesn't help ... when they beat up an opposition presidential candidate, not when there are so many issues of concern to the OSCE -- the objective, independent, international monitor ... And I can say that these elections don't help," he said.
Croatia "wants to be judged as a European country (and so) we're holding them to those very high standards ... And he's (Tudjman) not meeting a lot of those standards," Burns said.

"We do have greater expectations for Tudjman and Croatia than we do for (Serbian President Slobodan) Milosevic, say, who is not someone who is being considered for anybody's club in Europe," he added.
